brief: First impressions of a product, and the ninety seconds that decide them

slots.eyebrow: On the ninety seconds that decide it
slots.subtitle: Six things that decide what somebody thinks of a product in the time it takes to scroll once.
slots.plate1Body: Answering one question: what is this, and is it for me.
slots.plate2Body: Usually describing an ambition instead of a category.
slots.coverNote: The last page is why the other five have a ceiling

slots.titleAccent: until they know what it is.
slots.body: Before a single feature registers, a person is answering one question: what is this and is it for me. Everything above the fold is spent on that question whether you meant it to be or not, and a headline about your ambition answers a question nobody asked.
slots.plate1Body: 'Invoicing for freelancers' beats any promise about the future.
slots.plate2Body: If it is for everyone, the reader assumes it is for somebody else.
slots.plate3Body: One honest screen outperforms three sentences of description.

slots.body: Evaluation is elimination. The reader is scanning for the disqualifier — wrong price, wrong platform, wrong size of company — and hiding it does not remove it, it just moves the disappointment further down where it costs more.
slots.plate1Body: Hiding it converts curiosity into resentment, reliably.
slots.plate2: Name who it is not for
slots.plate2Body: It builds more trust than any claim about who it is for.
slots.plate3Body: The one you dread is the one they are already thinking.

slots.body: Testimonials read as decoration because they are unfalsifiable. What survives scepticism is anything the reader can verify without leaving the page — a number with a method, a name they recognise, or the product doing the thing in front of them.
slots.plate1Body: A working demo settles what a paragraph cannot.
slots.plate2Body: An unnamed quote is worth less than no quote.
slots.plate3Body: 'Fourteen minutes' is believed. 'Blazing fast' is not.

slots.body: Three plans is a comparison. Six is a research project, and the reader who cannot decide does not pick carefully — they postpone, which in practice means never. Reducing the choice is usually worth more than improving any single option.
slots.plate1Body: Say which and why. It is the whole job of a pricing page.
slots.plate2Body: Nobody has ever chosen it and it costs every reader time.
slots.plate3Body: Two buttons of equal weight is a question, not an offer.

slots.body: Vague language signals that you have not done the work, regardless of whether you have. The detail that seems too small to mention is precisely the thing that convinces, because only somebody who has done it would know to say it.
slots.plate1Body: Even unimpressive ones. Especially unimpressive ones.
slots.plate2Body: Mentioning what is hard proves you have met it.
slots.plate3Body: Remove 'incredibly' and the sentence gets more credible.

slots.body: Presentation raises the ceiling on something people already want and does nothing to the floor. A first impression that is honest and clear will get you found out faster, which is the correct outcome and never the one anybody is hoping for.
slots.plate1Body: Good or bad, you learn sooner. That is the value.
slots.plate2: Do not dress up a maybe
slots.plate2Body: A confused product presented clearly looks confused.
slots.plate3Body: Then the page is worth the afternoon it takes.

slots.eyebrow: On the page you already have
slots.titleAccent: and say who it is for.
slots.body: Two changes, both of which take twenty minutes, and between them they answer the only two questions a new reader is actually asking.
slots.plate1Body: Twenty minutes, and the comfort of being vague.
slots.plate2Body: A faster verdict, which is the only thing you can act on.
slots.signoff: Being found out sooner is the point
